153.t: Big Sid Catlett and Jo Jones on brushes and keeping 'one'
153.s: His main teachers' advice on brushes and never losing one.
153.q: Yeah. Well my two main teachers were Big Sid Catlett and Jo Jones. I had a chance to see Chick [Webb] once but Big Sid and Jo really called me aside and said “look, here’s how you play the brushes, here’s how you do this, here’s how you do this, and always remember, don’t ever lose one.” You know I…

153.t: Lessons from Murray Spivack and the numbering of rudiments
153.s: Spivack made him go back to basics with a practice pad, and Bellson explains his own chart of how rolls are really built of bounces and taps.
153.ch: More drummers, teachers and advice for students
153.q: Yeah. Murray Spivack took me through that book. I thought I was a good player before I went to study with Murray Spivack. Somebody recommended him. I went up to see him in North Hollywood. He said, “Okay.” He says, “I want you to play for me on a practice pad.” He said, “Play me a single-stroke…

922.t: Tio's method of keeping time with the foot
922.s: Tio taught foot-tapping for time, then to feel it internally.
922.q: He did teach how to keep in time. He said, of course, as time go along, he wanted us to count with our footmen that he would teach us. That was to keep us right there that we wouldn't vary. He said, but then we must remember after we reached a certain stage and if we ever got to where we were…

448.t: Bechet's lessons: variations, scales, swinging and foot-patting
448.s: Bechet focused on variations, phrasing and swing, taught Raggin' the Scale, and said to carry your own rhythm section in your head.
448.q: Yeah, it went... That was an old Raggin'. I remember that. He taught me this because now you get a chance to practice your scales, but you can swing them too, you know.

1039.t: Length of lessons and Bechet's advice on fingers, mind and rhythm
1039.s: Lessons lasted from half an hour to an afternoon depending on his mood. Bechet advised coordinating mind and fingers and bringing out rhythm.
1039.q: they'd last all afternoon or they'd last only half an hour depending on how he felt and uh uh actually physically yeah you know if he had a hard uh session the night before and was very tired

825.s: Metoyer's French method taught foot-tapping as an imaginary needle for time. Ernie compares his two-beat down-and-up system with other teachers' four-beat counts.
825.q: Oh yeah, I mean, that French Pochelon method, I've never seen nobody here with one like that. Of course, they have those diagrams now, made in a circle with your arrows pointing each way to show you. And with the dialect in the center, with the time on it, see? And you'll have in your mind an…

787.t: Teaching students the feeling of time
787.s: He teaches students to play with Bud Powell and Armstrong recordings slowed down to feel how they push and pull time; the feeling, he says, is rhythm, not intellect.
787.q: I have — with a few I have, yeah. But that’s the experience of improvising jazz with that feeling. So most of them that I have don’t know how to play that feeling so that [plays] it’s this bouncy triplet kind of thing where there’s another way of playing jazz eighth notes that sink into the time,…

341.t: Practice: push/pull technique and drum studies
341.s: She describes technical practice, including the Brazilian push/pull eighth-note technique, and checking out Max Roach, Elvin Jones and Philly Joe Jones.
341.q: Oh my gosh, well I spend a lot of time working on different, and this is recently, just different technical things and technical approaches. Like there’s a lot more than one way to hit a drum, this way, there’s using your fingers, there’s using every finger, there’s stick placement, there’s wrist…

413.t: Cootie Williams and the foot-tapping cure
413.s: Cootie advises Maxwell to practice with both feet marching, using Arban exercise 10.
413.ch: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
413.q: But over the years I've been lucky to work with people like him I could learn things from. Like Cootie I learned an awful lot from. From the day I first met him in San Francisco when I was still in high school, 1932 or something --

112.t: Will Marion Cook teaches him to retard for a singer
112.s: He asks Will Marion Cook how to slow down with Abbie Mitchell and learns to bend his knees on each retard.
112.ch: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
112.q: : No, it was the Club Alabam's show. Just like The Cotton Club's show, it was called the Club Alabam's show. But this was a great show. And I learnt one thing, because Abby Mitchell was a great star in those days, you see. She could sing very well. Will Marion Cook used to come there because that…
